In summary, our research is concerned with

(1) the analysis of T cell epitopes in the 65‐Kd antigen from Mycobacterum bovis, (2) the influence of the H‐2 complex on the T cell recognition of these epitopes, and (3) the cross‐reactivity of these epitopes with the homologous E. coli protein.

the generation of T cell responses to the whole protein and to individual peptides, the influence of the MHC on T cell recognition and the extent of cross‐reactive responses to homologous and heterologous GroEL proteins.

the identification of T cell epitopes on the 65‐ kDa stress protein of M. bovis, the analysis of the role of major histocompatibility class II molecules in antigen presentation, and the generation of T cell responses by peptides.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the 65‐kd mycobacterial antigen is composed of a number of epitopes, some of which are recognized by several H2‐disparate strains of mice and some of which can be recognized in a cross‐reacted manner by T cells specific for the homologous E. coli protein.

the pattern of T cell epitopes recognized by a given mouse strain is dependent on the H‐2 type of the strain, the sequence homology of the peptide with the native protein, and the major histoincompatibility complex molecule involved in peptide presentation.
T cell recognition of a protein antigen is a complex process involving the interaction of multiple determinants, each of which is influenced by the HLA haplotype.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

immunization with a peptide can induce a cross‐reactivity to the native protein in mice, but the extent of cross‐reactive response is determined by the peptide sequence and the major histompatibility complex class II molecules used to present the epitope.

the T cell epitope repertoire of a protein is influenced by the HLA‐II haplotype of the host, the sequence homology of the peptide to other molecules in the organism, and the sequence of the peptide itself.

the GroEL protein from M. bovis has several T cell determinants, that these determinants are recognized by several HLA‐disparate mouse haplotypes, that some of these epitopes can be presented by both H‐2‐E and H‐2‐A molecules, that the epitopes are located on the same region of the GroEL protein, that immunization with several of these peptides induces T cell cross‐reactivity with the homologous protein from E. coli,
The main takeaway from our work is that
immunization with peptides can be used to generate T cell responses to the native protein, and that the H‐2 restriction of the response can be influenced by immunization with peptides.
immunization with a single peptide can prime for a response to the native antigen.
the use of peptide immunization to generate T cell responses to proteins is feasible and may be useful for the development of new vaccines against infectious agents.
